purpose: Mercaptopurine is mainly used to treat a type of blood cancer called acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL). It is also sometimes used to help manage inflammatory bowel diseases like Crohn's disease. It helps keep certain conditions under control and can be part of a long-term treatment plan.
how_it_works: Your body's cells need certain building blocks to grow and multiply. Mercaptopurine works by blocking one of those building blocks, which slows down or stops the growth of cancer cells or overactive immune cells. Think of it like putting a roadblock in the way of cells that are growing too fast or causing harm.
common_side_effects: Nausea, vomiting, or upset stomach are common, especially when you first start. You may also notice loss of appetite, mouth sores, or diarrhea. It can lower your blood cell counts, which may make you feel tired or more likely to get infections.
warnings: This medication can seriously lower your immune system, making it harder to fight infections — so tell your doctor right away if you have a fever, chills, or feel unusually sick. It can also affect your liver, so regular blood tests are very important. Avoid live vaccines while taking this medicine. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, talk to your doctor, as this drug can harm an unborn baby. Some people have a genetic variation that makes them process this drug differently, so your doctor may test you before starting.
typical_dosing: The dose is very individualized and depends on your body weight, the condition being treated, and how your body handles the medication. It is usually taken once a day by mouth, often in tablet or liquid form. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never adjust your dose on your own.
